dtz.lead: The final exam of a state-funded integration course — result at level A2 or B1.
dtz.who.title: Who is the DTZ for?
dtz.who.text: The DTZ comes at the end of an integration course and matters to many immigrants in Germany — among other things as proof of German for a permanent residence permit. Depending on the score reached, either level A2 or level B1 is certified.
dtz.fmt.ads.what: Match short adverts to the people they suit
dtz.fmt.tf.what: Understand a newspaper article and judge statements about it
dtz.fmt.forum.what: Match statements to people; understand an interview
dtz.fmt.form.what: Transfer information from an e-mail into a form
dtz.fmt.write.what: A personal reply e-mail + a formal letter
dtz.fmt.speak.what: Describe a picture, then answer personal follow-up questions
dtz.fmt.speak.source: Our own classroom material — 90 sec. describing + 90 sec. follow-up questions
dtz.format.note: The task types above come from our own DTZ classroom material, which also feeds our interactive reading & writing and speaking exercises. We have no source of our own for the exam's official total duration — check the BAMF/telc model set for that.
dtz.scoring.title: How the DTZ is scored
dtz.scoring.text: There is no single percentage pass mark. Listening and reading are scored together: 20 listening tasks and 25 reading tasks make 45 points. From 33 points level B1 is certified, from 20 points A2. Writing and speaking are scored separately — each is also reported as A2 or B1. That is why a certificate can read, for example, "listening/reading B1, writing A2".
dtz.set.title: A complete practice set in exam format
dtz.set.text: Nine exam parts, 45 scored tasks — listening parts 1–4 and reading parts 1–5, plus the writing task. At the end comes the evaluation against the official point thresholds, broken down by exam part. Progress stays saved in the browser.
dtz.mock.title: Shorter: mock reading test (tasks 1–4)
dtz.mock.text: All four reading tasks of the DTZ simulation as one continuous test with an overall result at the end — from real DTZ classroom material.
dtz.practice.intro: All five practice tools come from real DTZ classroom material — the richest exercises on the whole site.
telc.lead: The European Language Certificates — a modular exam system recognised by many employers, authorities and some universities.
telc.who.title: Who is telc for?
telc.who.text: There is a telc exam for almost every CEFR level. They are often required for employment, residence permits and — in the university variants — for admission to a degree course. There are also occupational and specialist versions (telc Deutsch Beruf, Pflege, Medizin); this page deliberately does not cover those — it is about general German.
telc.sprachbausteine.note: Sprachbausteine are telc's speciality: grammar and vocabulary are not asked in isolated sentences but inside a running text. Not every telc exam has all five subtests — telc A1 (Start Deutsch 1) tests listening, reading and writing together and has no Sprachbausteine. From B1 they are part of it.
telc.moreLevels.title: Other levels
telc.moreLevels.text: Above is the telc exam we have a practice test for as a source. Times, task counts and pass marks differ considerably between levels — for A2, B1, B2, C1 or C2 please check the official telc model set for your module. We enter here only what we can document, rather than estimating figures.
telc.sb.title: Practise Sprachbausteine
telc.sb.text: The exam part that exists in this form only at telc: part 1 as matching from a word box, part 2 as multiple choice inside a running text — with everyday texts and instant marking.
telc.a1.title: A complete practice set at A1
telc.a1.text: telc Deutsch A1 and Goethe A1 are the same exam — Start Deutsch 1. A whole practice set in exam format: listening, reading and writing, with progress per exam part and marking against the official pass mark.
telc.practice.intro: These tools are useful across levels and exams. They come from the DTZ classroom material and test general article, grammar and vocabulary knowledge — not telc-specific task formats.
goethe.lead: The Goethe-Institut's own exams — recognised worldwide for visas, study and employers.
goethe.who.title: Who is the Goethe-Zertifikat for?
goethe.who.text: Unlike telc, each Goethe-Zertifikat is a standalone exam for exactly one level (e.g. Goethe-Zertifikat B1, not "B1 or B2"). Goethe-Zertifikat A1 ("Start Deutsch 1") is often required for spousal reunification; higher levels are used for study, work and naturalisation.
goethe.moreLevels.text: Above is the level we have a practice set for as a source. Times, task counts and pass marks differ considerably between A1 and C2 — for A2, B1, B2, C1 or C2 please check the Goethe-Institut's official model set. We enter here only what we can document, rather than estimating figures.
goethe.a1.title: At A1, practise for telc at the same time
goethe.a1.text: Start Deutsch 1 is a joint exam of the Goethe-Institut and telc — the oral part is identical in both (introducing yourself · asking for information · making requests). The telc page shows the same exam with its point distribution and grading scale.
goethe.practice.intro: These tools are useful across levels and exams. They come from the DTZ classroom material and test general article, grammar and vocabulary knowledge — not Goethe-specific task formats.
testdaf.lead: Test Deutsch als Fremdsprache — the standard proof of German for university study in Germany.
testdaf.who.title: Who is TestDaF for?
testdaf.who.text: TestDaF is aimed above all at international applicants to universities: the result is the usual proof of German for admission to German universities. Unlike Goethe or telc there is no "level you book" — everyone sits the same exam, and each of the four skills is graded separately with a TestDaF level (TDN 3, 4 or 5).
testdaf.fmt.schreiben.what: One coherent text about a chart or statistic
testdaf.format.note: There is no simple percentage pass mark — each skill is graded separately as TDN 3, 4 or 5, and universities decide for themselves which combination they require. We have no TestDaF source material of our own; the figures here are widely known, public information about the exam format, not invented details. For the exact current times, check the official TestDaF model set.
testdaf.set.title: Practise reading comprehension in exam format
testdaf.set.text: Three reading tasks in the order of the real exam — matching, multiple choice, and yes/no/not in the text — plus the writing task about a chart, with structure, set phrases and a checklist. We have no TestDaF source material: the structure is publicly known knowledge about the format, all texts and tasks are written by us and are nowhere presented as official exam material. Listening is still missing — for that we need audio recordings.
testdaf.practice.intro: Besides the practice set above, these three tools are useful across levels and exams — they come from the DTZ classroom material but test general article, grammar and vocabulary knowledge, not TestDaF-specific content.

lid.who.text: Unlike telc, Goethe, TestDaF or the DTZ, "Leben in Deutschland" does not test a level of German but knowledge of society, history and the legal order — it is a prerequisite for naturalisation and often closes the orientation course of an integration course.

grammatik.artikel.intro: Every German noun has a gender — and the gender is not in the word itself but in the article in front of it. That is why you never learn „Tisch“, always „der Tisch“.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: With no question word, the verb slides right to the front: „Er kommt aus Berlin.“ becomes „Kommt er aus Berlin?“ And a negative question is answered not with ja but with doch.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: A W-question starts with the question word, the verb follows immediately in position 2 — and the subject slides in behind it. Once you see the pattern, every question comes out right.
grammatik.praesens.intro: The verb adapts to the person: ich lern-e, du lern-st, er lern-t. The stem stays, only the ending changes — and sein and haben go their own way.
grammatik.plural.intro: In the plural the article is always die — but the noun has five ways of becoming more: -e, -er, -(e)n, -s or no ending at all, often with an umlaut.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? mein Buch, dein Auto, ihre Tasche. The possessive article takes the same endings as ein/eine — it just also says who something belongs to.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Requests, instructions, tips: the imperative puts the verb first. With du the pronoun drops out, with Sie it stays — and a bitte makes everything friendlier.
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: Nominative → accusative: der → den, die → die, das → das, die (pl.) → die. After haben, brauchen, sehen.
grammatik.dativ.intro: Dative pronouns: ich→mir, du→dir, er/es→ihm, sie→ihr, wir→uns, ihr→euch, sie/Sie→ihnen/Ihnen. Definite article: der/das→dem, die→der.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: müssen, können, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen — they say not what happens but how it is meant: obligation, permission, ability or wish. The second verb moves to the end of the sentence.
grammatik.negation.intro: Two words share the work of negating: „kein“ replaces „ein“ in front of a noun, „nicht“ negates everything else. And „nicht“ almost always sits further right than you expect.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: In conversation, the past is told in the Perfekt. Two questions to settle: which auxiliary verb — and what is the Partizip II?
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: In a German statement the conjugated verb always stands in position 2 — whatever is in position 1. The second part of the verb waits at the end of the sentence: that is the Satzbrücke, the sentence bracket.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Nine prepositions can take either dative or accusative. The question decides: „Wo?“ means dative, „Wohin?“ means accusative. Im Kino is not ins Kino.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Some verbs need a fixed preposition. Learn the pattern, then practise it in five different task types — like a page from a coursebook.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: The prefix moves to the end of the sentence: fern|sehen, ein|steigen, aus|steigen, an|rufen, an|kommen.
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: In many languages the two are the same word — in German they are not. A single moment in the past is always „als“; anything repeated, conditional or future is „wenn“.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: A small group of masculine nouns adds -(e)n in every case except the nominative: der Herr, but an Herrn Schneider. Knowing them is what makes a letter come out right.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: The adjective's ending depends not on the noun but on what stands in front of it. Three types — definite article, indefinite article, no article — and the pattern is yours.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: An infinitive clause has no subject of its own — the main clause's subject carries over. The „zu“ sits right at the end before the infinitive, and inside the word with separable verbs.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: Three past tenses, three jobs: Perfekt for conversation, Präteritum for narrating and writing — and Plusquamperfekt for everything that happened before that.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: „Wo ist der Bahnhof?“ sounds curt. „Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?“ sounds polite — and turns the question into a subordinate clause with the verb at the end.
grammatik.passiv.intro: Active → passive with a modal verb: subject + modal + … + Partizip II + werden. "Ich buche das Hotel." → "Das Hotel muss gebucht werden."
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: Unreal wish or reproach in the past: hätte/wäre + Partizip II (+ sollen). "Was hättest du machen sollen?"
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from the word it refers back to, and its case from the relative clause. The verb goes at the end.
grammatik.irgend.intro: You don't know exactly, or it doesn't matter: just stick „irgend“ in front of a question word, the indefinite article or „welche“ — and the statement is comfortably vague.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: „Auch ich schenke dir Blumen“ and „Ich schenke dir auch Blumen“ say two different things. Focus particles sit directly in front of the part they highlight — and that changes the meaning.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Beyond nicht and kein there is a whole system: nichts, niemand, nirgendwo, noch nie, nicht mehr — plus the affixes un-, in- and -los, which negate a word from the inside.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: „Rücksicht nehmen“, „in Frage kommen“, „zur Verfügung stehen“ — fixed noun-plus-verb pairs in which the verb has almost no meaning of its own left. They have to be learnt whole.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: A whole sentence becomes one word: „Der Zug fährt ein“ → „der einfahrende Zug“. Partizip I means: happening right now. Partizip II means: finished, or done to it.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: These connectors always come in pairs: „nicht nur … sondern auch“, „weder … noch“, „je … desto“. Once you use the first half, you owe the second.
kultur.duzen-siezen.cardIntro: German has two words for "you": du and Sie.
kultur.pfand.cardIntro: You buy a bottle of water.
kultur.sonntagsruhe.cardIntro: On Sundays the shops in Germany are closed.
kultur.trinkgeld.cardIntro: In a restaurant in Germany you leave a small tip.
kultur.bundeslaender.cardIntro: Germany is a federal state: it consists of sixteen Länder, each with its own government, its own parliament and its own areas of responsibility.
kultur.feiertage.cardIntro: Public holidays in Germany are largely a matter for each individual Land.
kultur.muelltrennung.cardIntro: Waste in Germany is collected separately: paper, packaging, organic waste, residual waste and glass each go into a different container.
kultur.termine.cardIntro: For a great many things in Germany you make an appointment first: at the public office, the doctor, the hairdresser, sometimes even the phone shop.
kultur.anmeldung.cardIntro: Anyone moving into a home in Germany has to register: at the city's Einwohnermeldeamt or Bürgeramt.
kultur.krankenversicherung.cardIntro: Health insurance is compulsory in Germany: since 2009 every person must be insured.
kultur.mieten.cardIntro: Flat listings show several prices side by side, and the biggest of them is rarely the one you transfer each month.
kultur.schulsystem.cardIntro: Education in Germany is a matter for the individual Länder.
kultur.ausbildung.cardIntro: Alongside university, Germany has a second recognised route into a profession: the dual apprenticeship.
kultur.kuendigung.cardIntro: An employment relationship in Germany rarely ends informally.
Germany has public-service broadcasters such as ARD and ZDF (plus many regional and radio stations).
kultur.vereine.cardIntro: A large part of leisure life in Germany is organised — in clubs, the Vereine.
kultur.foederalismus.cardIntro: Ask about "the government" in Germany and you will often get a question back: which one? The federal state distributes responsibilities across three levels, and not by the size of the task but along an order laid down in the Grundgesetz.
kultur.sozialversicherung.cardIntro: Every German payslip lists a series of deductions that together come to far more than the income tax.
kultur.wahlen.cardIntro: The German ballot paper has two columns, and most misunderstandings about German elections begin with the left one looking more important than the right.
kultur.erinnerungskultur.cardIntro: Few areas are as hard for newcomers to place as Germany's handling of the Nazi period, because it is anchored at once in law, in schooling, in the look of its cities and in everyday language.
kultur.grundgesetz.cardIntro: That Germany's constitution is called „Grundgesetz“ and not „Verfassung“ was meant in 1949 as a stopgap — and the name stayed.
kultur.mitbestimmung.cardIntro: Wages in Germany are to a considerable extent set neither by the legislature nor in the individual contract, but negotiated between associations that the state deliberately does not interfere with.

wissen.rights.p1: Everything in this knowledge base is written by DeutschAcademy and generated from this site's own data. None of it is scanned, copied or excerpted from a textbook — which is exactly why we are allowed to give it away. Every file states its origin at the bottom.
wissen.rights.p2: What deliberately is NOT here: audio and book files from publishers (Hueber, Klett, Cornelsen, telc). We are not allowed to pass those on, not free of charge and not in class either. Official model sets we link instead where they are published — see "Official materials".
hoeren.a1-ansage-bahnhof.blurb: Gleis, Verspätung, Minuten — the three words you actually hear at a station.
hoeren.a1-anruf-arzt.blurb: A surgery cancels an appointment and offers a new one. Note down the day and the time.
hoeren.a1-supermarkt.blurb: Asking the way inside a shop. Left, right, at the back — and what is out of stock.
hoeren.a1-verabredung.blurb: Two friends arrange to meet. Time, place and a small last-minute change.
hoeren.a2-amt-termin.blurb: An appointment at the immigration office no longer works. What to say on the phone — and what to bring.
hoeren.a2-wohnungsbesichtigung.blurb: Kaltmiete, Nebenkosten, Kaution — the numbers you decide on in that quarter of an hour.
hoeren.a2-radio-wetter-verkehr.blurb: Two short bulletins one after the other. Numbers, directions and a warning.
hoeren.a2-paketdienst.blurb: Two messages on the voicemail. Who called, what should you do, by when?
hoeren.b1-krankmeldung.blurb: Calling in sick without apologising — and knowing from when the doctor's note is due.
hoeren.b1-elterngespraech.blurb: A teacher and a father talk about marks, homework and a recommendation.
hoeren.b1-radio-muelltrennung.blurb: Which bin for what — and why the yellow bin is the commonest mistake.
hoeren.b1-durchsage-ersatzverkehr.blurb: The S-Bahn is cancelled. Anyone who has somewhere to be needs to listen closely now.
hoeren.b2-diskussion-homeoffice.blurb: Three positions, one compromise. Spotting the arguments — and who ends up conceding what.
hoeren.b2-interview-anerkennung.blurb: An advisor explains what „Gleichwertigkeit" means — and what the commonest mistake in the process is.
hoeren.b2-beschwerde-versicherung.blurb: A claim has been refused. How to stay polite and still not give way.
hoeren.b2-vortrag-ehrenamt.blurb: Figures, a trend and a thesis. Telling the main claim from the example.
lesen.a1-schilder-im-haus.blurb: Six notices in the stairwell — what is allowed where?
lesen.a1-nachricht-einladung.blurb: Who, when, where — and what should you bring?
lesen.a2-wohnungsanzeigen.blurb: Four listings, four people looking — who fits with whom?
lesen.a2-email-kurs-absage.blurb: The course is cancelled. What exactly does that mean now?
lesen.b1-digitales-buero.blurb: A circular from management — three statements, true or false?
lesen.b1-anzeigen.blurb: Five situations, six adverts — one is left over.
lesen.b1-zeitungsartikel.blurb: One article, five statements — true or false?
lesen.b1-interview.blurb: An interview with gaps — which answer fits?
lesen.b2-artikel-homeoffice.blurb: Two studies, two results — and what the text actually claims about them.
lesen.b2-kommentare-innenstadt.blurb: Five comments, five stances — who argues with what?
schreiben.a1-formular-anmeldung.blurb: Ten fields, one short text — the commonest writing task in everyday life.
schreiben.a1-nachricht-absage.blurb: Turning something down in three sentences: reason, regret, new suggestion.
schreiben.a2-email-nachbarn.blurb: Asking for something politely — with „könnten Sie“ instead of „Sie müssen“.
schreiben.a2-formular-arztpraxis.blurb: One phone call, one form — and two details that are not stated word for word in the text.
schreiben.b1-brief-david.blurb: Four guide points, one semi-formal letter.
schreiben.b1-fehlerjagd.blurb: First find the mistakes in someone else's text — then you start seeing them in your own.
schreiben.b2-beschwerde-reiseveranstalte: Staying factual and still making a demand — the hardest tone at B2.
sprechenSet.a1-zuhause.blurb: Four pictures from your immediate surroundings: kitchen, shop, station, playground.
sprechenSet.a2-unterwegs.blurb: Four pictures in which several people are doing something together.
sprechenSet.b1-arbeit.blurb: Four situations to do with work, job applications and public offices.
sprechenSet.b2-gesellschaft.blurb: Four pictures you have to take a position on, not just describe.
sprechen.a1-sich-vorstellen.blurb: The very first speaking task — and the one you need most often in daily life.
sprechen.a1-bild-bahnhof.blurb: Who? Where? What is the person doing? Three questions, three sentences.
sprechen.a1-bild-kueche.blurb: Two people, one evening meal — and the words that come up every day around it.
sprechen.a1-bild-supermarkt.blurb: Shopping — numbers, groceries and the word „bezahlen“.
sprechen.a1-bild-spielplatz.blurb: Children, parents, weather — and the first chance to use „weil“.
sprechen.a2-bild-gartenarbeit.blurb: Describe, interpret, and then talk about your own experience.
sprechen.a2-bild-bus.blurb: Describing a mood — and saying how you get to work yourself.
sprechen.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfest.blur: Many people in one picture — and the question of why they are there.
sprechen.a2-bild-wartezimmer.blurb: Waiting, appointments, impatience — and the word „Krankenkasse“.
sprechen.b1-bild-rolltreppe.blurb: Interpreting a situation, not just listing what is in it.
sprechen.b1-bild-bewerbungsgespraech.blu: Two sides of a table — and the question of who is actually nervous here.
sprechen.b1-bild-werkstatt.blurb: Apprenticeship, skilled trades and the question of why too few people take this route.
sprechen.b1-bild-buergeramt.blurb: Take a number, wait, fill the form — and how to talk about it without complaining.
sprechen.b2-vortrag-ehrenamt.blurb: Picture, short talk, discussion — the three stages on one topic.
sprechen.b2-diskussion-ehrenamt-schule.b: Take a position, take up the counter-argument, hold your ground.
sprechen.b2-planen-abschiedsfeier.blurb: Suggest, refuse, agree — the task where you have to react rather than present.
sprechen.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.blurb: A likeable picture — and the question of who can afford it.
sprechen.b2-bild-videokonferenz.blurb: Four in the room, four on the screen — and who gets lost in between.
sprechen.b2-bild-baustelle-innenstadt.bl: Building work, diversions, irritation — and the question of who a city belongs to.
sprechen.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.blurb: Sorting, collecting, disposing — and whether it achieves anything at all.

sprechenB1B2.note: Oral exam B1/B2: three stages per topic — describing a picture, a short talk, a discussion. The three-stage format comes from 'Pruefungsvorbereitung B1-B2 muendliche Pruefung Bild 1-6.pdf'; its six topics are nursing-specific and belong in an occupational course, not here. The topics here cover the usual general-language exam areas (environment, housing, media, health, education, living together). Images: assets from the repo.
dtzSet.sourceNote: DeutschAcademy's own practice set, built to the official DTZ format: nine exam parts, 45 scored tasks (listening 1–20, reading 21–45), two writing tasks. Task counts, task types and marking match the real exam — the texts and tasks themselves are our own, not taken from an official practice set.
telcSb.sourceNote: Task types modelled on telc: matching from a word box (more words than gaps, each used only once) and multiple choice within the text. Exactly how many tasks an exam part has varies by level — for that, the official model set for your module applies. The texts and tasks here are our own, not exam tasks.
